# Nautical charts and map projections (portolans, Ptolemy, Mercator) (`map_projection_charts`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by round_earth_size, world_geography, latitude_astrolabe_quadrant, magnetic_compass, trigonometry
- Core idea: A chart is a calculating tool: portolan charts draw coasts with a web of compass lines (rhumbs) from wind roses, so a pilot reads the course with a ruler and the distance with dividers, which works in the Mediterranean but distorts large oceans because they ignore the curve of the Earth. On a sphere the meridians converge, so one degree of longitude shrinks with the cosine of latitude (111 km at the equator, 56 km at 60°); Mercator (1569) spaces the parallels ever wider towards the poles so that every line of constant true bearing is straight, at the price of making high latitudes look huge. For the player in Florence: Ptolemy's grid of latitude and longitude was revived here (Latin translation by Jacopo Angeli, c. 1406–10), and Martellus' world map of c. 1490 already shows Dias's Cape.
- Pitfalls:
  - Using a flat plane chart over thousands of kilometres; east–west distances at 40° are overstated by about 30 per cent
  - Reading areas on a Mercator map (Greenland is not the size of Africa)
  - Thinking a straight line on a Mercator chart is the shortest route; it is a constant course (rhumb line), the shortest is a great circle
  - Assuming medieval maps were all symbolic T-O maps; portolan charts of c. 1300 are remarkably accurate for the Mediterranean
- History: china: 3rd c. – Pei Xiu's grid principles; 1136 Yu ji tu, a grid map carved in stone; Zheng He's route chart survives in the Wubei zhi (1621); greece: c. 150 AD – Ptolemy's Geography with latitude, longitude and two projections; islamic: 1154 – al-Idrisi's world map for Roger II of Sicily; 1513 Piri Reis map with the Atlantic coasts; europe: c. 1275 – Carta Pisana, oldest surviving portolan; 1406–10 Ptolemy in Latin (Florence); 1477 and 1482 printed Ptolemies (Bologna, Ulm, Florence); c. 1490 Martellus; 1492 Behaim's globe; 1500 Juan de la Cosa's chart with America; 1507 Waldseemüller names America; 1569 Mercator; 1599 Edward Wright gives the mathematics
- Read:
  - J. B. Harley and David Woodward (eds), The History of Cartography, vol. 1 (1987)
  - Mark Monmonier, Rhumb Lines and Map Wars: A Social History of the Mercator Projection (2004)
  - Edward Wright, Certaine Errors in Navigation (1599)
